place.zh: 外门演武场 · 五行台
place.en: The outer court training ground · the Five Elements Platform

setup.zh: 你站在台边，把那只手翻过来，低头看着自己的掌心。
setup.en: You stand at the edge of the platform, turn that hand over, and look down at your palm.

recap.zh: 你的掌心烙下一个印子：一个圈，圈里一横，搓不掉。决赛，九层的祁长松站在台心「我不碰你」，土盾吃尽了你的法术；香只剩一指，他出了掌，你挨住了，把猪蜻蜓拍在他背上——风掉头，两个人一齐飞起来，撞了两棵老柏；他撕了符，一只脚落在台边，你倒挂在西角的柏树上。「……祁长松，胜。」筑基丹归了他；观主对你说：「前四，进内门名册。」
recap.en: A mark was branded in your palm: a circle with a bar across it, and it won't rub off. In the final Qi Changsong, layer nine, stood at the centre — "I won't touch you" — and his earth shield ate every spell you threw; with one finger of incense left he struck, you took the palm and slapped the pig-copter on his back — the wind turned, the two of you flew up together and banged off both old cypresses; he tore the charm and landed on one foot at the edge, and you hung upside down in the west cypress. "…Qi Changsong wins." The Foundation pill went to him; the abbot told you: "The last four go into the inner register."

zh: 掌心正中，烙着一个印子。
en: In the middle of the palm, a brand.
A circle, with a bar across it.

story.zh:
小满站起身来，把那只手翻过来，低头看着自己的掌心。

掌心正中，烙着一个印子。不红，不肿，是一道一道发白的细线，像是从肉里头长出来的：一个圈，圈里一横。

他拿拇指去搓，搓不掉；拿指甲去刮，刮得皮都红了，那个圈，那一横，还在那里，白白的，凉凉的。

胸口的木牌凉了下来，一个很低的声音在他耳朵里道：「……你拿手接了。」小满小声道：「嗯。」那声音隔了很久，才又道：「……傻子。」便没有声息了。

褚先生站在人群最后头，一只手捋着山羊胡子，捋到一半，停在半空。隔了好一会儿，才有一个声音怯生生地道：「……他……他那是……反噬了吧？」这一声给众人打开了一扇门：「对对对，反噬！吃丹吃坏了！」「一夜吞了三瓶丹，灵力是虚的！」「褚先生讲过的，轻则退三层，重则废！」「我就说他脸上那些斑不对劲！」越说越信，越信越觉得自己早就看出来了。褚先生的山羊胡子终于落了下来，他咳了一声，沉着脸道：「丹药之道，贪多必失。诸位引以为戒。」说罢转身走了，走的时候，回头看了小满一眼，看的是他垂在身边的那只手。台角的执事这才想起手里的锣，敲了一下：「马小宝不能再打了。沈小满，胜。」

当时谁也没去想，一个四层，怎么接得住那一镜。褚先生之外，还有两个人没跟着说反噬。一个是台北面竹椅上的观主玄沉子，他从头到尾没动过，这时候却轻轻「嗯」了一声。另一个是山门台阶上的瞿老，他背对着演武场，一直在扫地；镜子裂开的那一声，他的扫帚停了，停在半道上。那三百级台阶，他扫了五十年，这一天，没有扫完。
story.en:
Xiaoman stood up, turned his hand over, and looked down at his palm.

In the middle of the palm a mark was branded. Not red, not swollen: fine white lines, as if they had grown out of the flesh — a circle, with a bar across it.

He rubbed it with his thumb and it didn't rub off; he scraped it with a nail till the skin went red, and the circle, the bar, were still there, white, cold.

The token on his chest cooled, and a very low voice said in his ear: "…You caught it with your hand." "Mm," he whispered. A long while later the voice said: "…Fool." And then nothing.

At the very back, Master Chu stood with a hand on his goatee, stopped halfway down. After a long while a timid voice said: "…He… that was… backlash, wasn't it?" That opened a door: "Yes, yes, backlash! Ate too many pills!" "Three bottles in one night — his power's hollow!" "Master Chu told us — at best you drop three layers, at worst you're crippled!" "I knew those blotches weren't right!" The more they said it the more they believed it, and the more they believed it the surer they were they'd seen it all along. Master Chu's goatee finally came down. He coughed, and said sternly: "In the way of pills, greed brings loss. Take warning, all of you." He turned to go, and going, looked back once at Xiaoman — at the hand hanging at his side. Only then did the steward at the corner remember the gong in his hand, and struck it once: "Ma Xiaobao can't go on. Shen Xiaoman wins."

At the time, nobody stopped to wonder how a layer four had caught that flash. Besides Master Chu, two others didn't join in the talk of backlash. One was the abbot Xuanchenzi in the bamboo chair north of the stage; he hadn't moved the whole time, but now he gave a soft "Mm." The other was Old Qu on the gate steps, his back to the training ground, sweeping all along; at the sound of the mirror cracking his broom stopped, stopped halfway. That stair of three hundred steps he had swept for fifty years; that day, he never finished it.

label.zh: 攥着拳上台：决赛，对祁长松
label.en: Up with your fist hidden: the final, against Qi Changsong

exits.means: the final against Qi Changsong, layer nine, who will not touch him: spells eaten by his earth shield, the palm taken at the last finger of incense, the pig-copter slapped on his back, both flown into the cypresses — he lands on one foot at the edge and wins; no pill

story.zh:
日头挨着西边山尖的时候，另一个半边也打完了。内门那个七层把一套掌法在祁长松身上打了三遍，打得满头大汗，自己认了输。

决赛，沈小满对祁长松。

小满上台的时候，右手攥着拳，藏在袖子里，左臂上的布条已经红透了。祁长松已经站在了台心，两只脚钉在那道拼缝上，袍角都不动。他四十来岁，脸是方的，一双眼睛半睁半闭，看了一眼小满的袖子，道：「马师弟那一镜，你接了。」小满道：「他自己照干了。」祁长松道：「我不碰你。」说完，眼皮一垂，再不说话。香点着了。

我不碰你——台下的人都当是瞧不起。阿禾那张纸上写的是：没法打，认输。她看的是底册，小满看的是脚。他看了他一上午的脚，知道不是瞧不起。祁长松是土行的灵根，他那两只脚，是一身土行的法力扎进了石头里，扎了二十年；他一出手，那股土气便要跟着手走，分量往前一送，脚底下那一点，便松了。他不碰人，是他不能碰。

可知道是一回事。小满先扔法术：一颗火弹，一根冰锥，一道金刃，一样一样打过去。祁长松身前浮起一面土黄的光，像一面盾，火弹、冰锥、金刃撞上去，便似石子丢进泥塘，连个响都没有，叫它吃了。小满又扔木藤——木吃土——藤尖在那面光上扎出一个白点，便软了：四层的木，啃不动九层的土。台下的人起先还替他叫一声，叫到后来，不叫了。小满绕着他走了一圈，又走了一圈。他上去推，推他的胳膊，像推一根柱子；他抱住祁长松的腰往外扳，扳得脸都红了，祁长松低头看看他，像看一只扒在树干上的猴子。他退开三步，一头撞上去，撞在那人胸口上，像撞在一堵墙上，自己弹回来，摔在青石板上，左臂的伤口迸开了，血洒了一地。他爬起来，又撞，又弹回来，又摔。撞到第五回，他鼻子里、嘴里都是血，站起来的时候，晃了两晃。祁长松从头到尾没动过一根指头，他身上的血，全是自己撞出来的。

台下起先还笑：「四层的，下来吧，别耽误人家吃晚饭！」笑到后来，没人笑了。有人喊：「别撞了！」又有人喊：「撞他！」喊着喊着，喊「撞他」的越来越多。香，烧过一半了。

小满站在台边喘气，从怀里摸出一个油纸包，抽出一张黄纸来。台下的人伸长了脖子：一只猪，背上两对翅膀。「符？」「四层的人画的符？」「画的是猪？」祁长松那双半睁半闭的眼睛，睁开了。他的神识从那张纸上扫过去，扫了个空——一丝灵气也没有；可这个孩子捧着它，像捧着一件宝贝，这个孩子方才接裂了一面镜子。九层的人，最怕的就是神识读不出来的东西。小满没有往自己脑门上贴，只把那张纸攥在手心里，舔湿了背面，等着。

没有风。他攥着那张猪，等着。他爹说过，日头落山那一下，山里的风要掉个头——白天往山上走，夜里往山下走；掉头的那一下，林子里的鹿都要抬头。

香只剩一指的时候，日头沉下去了。演武场边上那面旗先是一垂，小满便动了。他不绕，不躲，直直地朝祁长松走过去，像一个打昏了头、只晓得往前走的孩子，那张黄纸攥在手里，朝前伸着。

祁长松的眉头，头一回皱了起来。二十年。他在这道拼缝上站了二十年，等这一颗丹等了二十年，香只剩一指了，这个浑身是血的四层，捏着一张他读不透的纸，还在往他跟前走；台下两百多人，喊的全是「撞他」。那张纸不能沾身。他的手，在袖子里动了一动。

祁长松出掌了。

小满看见了。他等的，就是这一掌。那一掌印上来之前，他怕得脚底发凉；印上来的那一霎，心里反倒静了，静得像蹲在雪地里等鹿。

那一掌不快，也不响，只是推了出来，平平地印在小满胸口上。大比不许伤人性命，这一掌量好了的：推得倒一个四层，推不死。可它落下来的那一霎，台下有人尖叫起来——小满整个人往后一折，一口血喷了出来，喷了祁长松一袖子。

他没有倒。

他的脚在青石板上往后犁出去半尺，脚底下那块地，却像生了根——秘境里那一撮土，在他丹田里长成的那一块厚地，存得住水，也挨得住这一掌。他晃着，弓着，就是没有倒，两只手往前一捞，一把揪住了祁长松的袍子，像一个挨了打、站不稳的孩子去抓旁边的大人。

祁长松这一掌推出去，扎在石头里的那股土气，跟着那一掌，全走到了手上；他后头那只脚，二十年来头一回，是轻的。

小满揪着他袍子的那只手，往他背上一拍。那张猪蜻蜓，贴在了祁长松的后背上。

便在这时，演武场边上那面旗「哗」地翻了个面。风掉头了。胸口的木牌极轻地暖了一暖，像有人在被窝里翻了个身，吹了一口气。

祁长松两只脚，离了地。

台下「啊」的一声，两百来张嘴一齐张开了。祁不动，在内门站了二十年、一步没挪过的祁不动，给一张画着猪的黄纸提了起来，一寸，两寸，脚尖离了那道拼缝。他到底是九层，身子一飘起来，一只手已闪电般反抓过来，一把揪住了小满的后领——要走，一块儿走。

两个人一齐飘了起来。

飘得并不好看。祁长松那张二十年没变过颜色的方脸，绿了又白，白了又绿；他头朝前，屁股朝后，一只手揪着小满，一只手往背上去够那张符；小满给他揪着领子，两条腿在半空里乱蹬，像一只叫人拎着后颈的猫。那猪蜻蜓认树，认准了演武场东角那棵老柏，一头撞了过去，「咚」的一声，弹回来；又认准了西角那棵，「咚」的一声，又弹回来。台下的人抱着脑袋四下乱躲，一个内门师兄的发髻给小满一脚踢歪了，他捂着脑袋在原地转了三圈，大叫：「我的头！我的头！」祁长松在半空里打了个转，总算够着了背上那张黄纸，「嘶」的一声，撕成了两半。

他撒了小满的领子，自己往下一落，落在五行台的边上，一只脚的脚尖点着石沿，另一只脚悬在外头，身子晃了一晃，又晃了一晃，袍袖张开像一只落枝的鹤，到底站住了。

小满没有落下来。西角那棵老柏的一根横杈，勾住了他的腰带。他头朝下，脚朝上，挂在半空里，晃荡着，鼻子里的血一滴一滴，往下滴。

便在这时，执事敲响了铜锣。那半炷香，到了。

执事看看台边上一只脚站着的那一个，又看看树上倒挂着的那一个，锣槌在手里转了两转，才道：「……祁长松，胜。」

那一声落下去，全场翻了天——一半是笑，「哈哈哈哈」，笑得前仰后合，笑得有人坐在地上捶腿，有人笑岔了气，一声接一声地打嗝；一半是吼，吼的是「祁不动动了！」「脚离地了！」「二十年，头一回！」笑声和吼声搅在一处，滚过五行台，滚过四棵老柏，滚得山门那边的鸟都飞了起来。

小满挂在树上，倒着看这一场。输了。他心里先是一空，一口气提了一整天，这时候泄了，泄得他连手指头都抬不起来。挂了一会儿，血往脑门上涌，他忽然觉得这样子实在好笑——一个四层，打了一天，打到最后，挂在树上，像他娘晾的一条咸鱼。他倒挂着，「噗」地笑出了声，跟着便「哈哈哈」地收不住了，一笑，肋下那根骨头一疼，又笑，又疼，笑得在树杈上一晃一晃，真像一条叫风吹着打秋千的咸鱼。

祁长松站在台边，一身的汗，袖子上是小满的血。他抬起头，看着树上倒挂着的那个孩子，看了很久，道：「二十年。头一回脚离地。」又道：「你那张符，哪来的？」小满在树上晃了一晃，倒着答：「……捡的。」祁长松看着他，没说信，也没说不信，冲他点了一点头，走下了台，走的时候，伸手把那个发髻歪了的师兄扶了一把。
story.en:
When the sun touched the western peaks, the other half was done too. The inner-court layer seven went through a whole set of palm strikes on Qi Changsong three times over, till the sweat poured off him, and yielded.

The final: Shen Xiaoman against Qi Changsong.

When Xiaoman went up, his right hand was a fist, hidden in his sleeve, and the cloth on his left arm was soaked red through. Qi Changsong already stood at the centre, feet nailed to the seam, not a fold of his robe stirring. He was about forty, square-faced, his eyes half open, half shut. He glanced at Xiaoman's sleeve. "Brother Ma's mirror — you caught it." "He shone himself dry." "I won't touch you," said Qi Changsong. And he lowered his eyelids and said no more. The incense was lit.

I won't touch you — everyone below took it for contempt. A He's page had said: can't be fought, concede. She had read the records; Xiaoman had read the feet. He had watched those feet all morning, and knew it wasn't contempt. Qi Changsong's root was earth, and those two feet were a whole body's earth power driven down into the stone, driven down for twenty years; the moment he struck, that earth would follow his hand, the weight would go forward, and the hold under his feet would loosen. He didn't touch people because he couldn't.

But knowing was one thing. Xiaoman threw spells first: a fire bolt, an ice spike, a metal blade, one after another. Before Qi Changsong rose an earth-yellow light like a shield, and fire, ice and metal struck it like pebbles dropped in a mud pond, without even a sound — it ate them. Xiaoman threw a wood vine — wood eats earth — and the vine's tip pricked one white dot on that light and went limp: layer four's wood couldn't gnaw layer nine's earth. Below, they cheered him at first; after a while they stopped. Xiaoman walked a circle round him, and another. He went in and pushed, pushed at his arm, like pushing a pillar; he hugged Qi Changsong round the waist and heaved outward till his face went red, and Qi Changsong looked down at him like a man looking at a monkey clinging to a tree trunk. He backed off three paces and rammed him headfirst, hit him in the chest like hitting a wall, bounced back, fell on the bluestone, and the wound in his left arm burst open and spattered blood over the stone. He got up, rammed again, bounced back again, fell again. By the fifth ram there was blood in his nose and his mouth, and when he stood he swayed twice. From first to last Qi Changsong never moved a finger; all the blood on Xiaoman he had rammed out of himself.

Below, they laughed at first: "Layer four, get down, don't keep the man from his supper!" After a while nobody laughed. Someone shouted: "Stop ramming!" Someone else: "Ram him!" And as they shouted, more and more were shouting "Ram him!" The incense was past half.

Xiaoman stood panting at the edge, took an oilpaper packet from his coat, and drew out a sheet of yellow paper. The crowd craned: a pig, with two pairs of wings on its back. "A charm?" "A charm drawn by a layer four?" "Is that a pig?" Qi Changsong's half-shut eyes opened. His spirit sense swept the paper and met nothing — not a wisp of spirit power; yet the boy held it like a treasure, and the boy had just cracked a mirror. What a layer nine fears most is the thing his spirit sense can't read. Xiaoman didn't stick it on his own forehead; he held the paper in his palm, licked its back wet, and waited.

No wind. He held the pig and waited. His father had said: the moment the sun goes behind the hill, the mountain wind turns round — by day it climbs, by night it runs downhill; and the moment it turns, every deer in the wood lifts its head.

With one finger of incense left, the sun went down. The banner at the edge of the training ground first sagged, and Xiaoman moved. He didn't circle, didn't dodge; he walked straight at Qi Changsong, like a child beaten senseless who only knows to keep walking forward, the yellow paper in his fist, held out in front.

For the first time Qi Changsong's brow knitted. Twenty years. Twenty years he had stood on that seam, twenty years he had waited for this pill, there was one finger of incense left, and this blood-soaked layer four, holding a paper he couldn't read, was still walking up to him; two hundred-odd below were all shouting "Ram him!" That paper must not touch him. His hand moved in his sleeve.

Qi Changsong struck.

Xiaoman saw it. This palm was what he'd been waiting for. Before it landed he was so afraid his soles went cold; the instant it landed, he went still inside, still as crouching in the snow waiting for a deer.

The palm was neither fast nor loud; it simply pushed out and pressed flat on Xiaoman's chest. No taking a life in the contest, and this palm was measured: enough to knock down a layer four, not enough to kill. But the instant it landed, someone below screamed — Xiaoman folded backward and a mouthful of blood sprayed out, all over Qi Changsong's sleeve.

He didn't fall.

His feet ploughed half a foot back across the bluestone, but the ground under them seemed to have taken root — the pinch of earth from the hidden realm, grown in his dantian into a thick piece of land, could hold water, and could take this palm too. He swayed, bent double, and did not fall; his two hands scooped forward and seized a fistful of Qi Changsong's robe, like a beaten child who can't stand grabbing the grown-up beside him.

As Qi Changsong's palm went out, the earth power driven into the stone went with it, all of it, into his hand; his back foot, for the first time in twenty years, was light.

The hand that held his robe gave his back a slap. The pig-copter was stuck to Qi Changsong's back.

At that moment the banner at the edge of the training ground flapped — whap — and turned over. The wind had turned. The token on his chest warmed, very faintly, as if someone under a quilt had rolled over and let out one breath.

Qi Changsong's feet left the ground.

Below, an "Ah!" — two hundred-odd mouths opening at once. Immovable Qi, who had stood twenty years in the inner court without moving a step, was being lifted by a yellow paper with a pig drawn on it, one inch, two inches, his toes leaving the seam. He was layer nine after all; as his body floated up, one hand snapped back like lightning and seized Xiaoman by the back of the collar — if he was going, they'd go together.

The two of them floated up together.

Not prettily. Qi Changsong's square face, which hadn't changed colour in twenty years, went green then white, white then green; he went head first, backside after, one hand gripping Xiaoman, the other groping at his back for the charm; Xiaoman, held by the collar, pedalled his legs in the air like a cat picked up by the scruff. The pig-copter knows trees: it fixed on the old cypress at the east corner and rammed straight into it — thunk — and bounced back; fixed on the one at the west corner — thunk — and bounced back again. Below, people ducked and scattered with their arms over their heads; one inner-court senior had his topknot kicked crooked by Xiaoman and clutched his head, spun three times on the spot, and yelled: "My head! My head!" Qi Changsong turned a circle in midair, got hold at last of the yellow paper on his back, and — rip — tore it in two.

He let go of Xiaoman's collar and dropped, landing on the edge of the platform, the toe of one foot on the stone rim, the other foot hanging out over nothing; he swayed once, and again, his sleeves spread like a crane alighting on a branch, and kept his footing.

Xiaoman didn't come down. A branch of the old cypress at the west corner caught his belt. He hung head down, feet up, in midair, swinging, blood dripping from his nose drop by drop.

At that moment the steward struck the gong. The half stick was done.

The steward looked at the one standing on one foot at the edge, then at the one hanging upside down in the tree, turned the gong-stick twice in his hand, and said: "…Qi Changsong wins."

The words fell, and the whole place erupted — half of it laughter — "Hahahaha!" — people doubled over, people sitting on the ground pounding their legs, people laughing so hard they got the hiccups, one hiccup after another; half of it roaring: "Immovable Qi moved!" "His feet left the ground!" "Twenty years, and the first time!" Laughter and roaring churned together, rolled over the Five Elements Platform, over the four old cypresses, till the birds over by the gate took off.

Xiaoman hung in the tree and watched it all upside down. Lost. First a hollow — a breath held all day, let out now, so he couldn't lift a finger. After hanging a while, with the blood rushing to his head, it suddenly struck him as too funny — a layer four, fighting all day, ending up hanging in a tree like a salted fish his mother had hung out to dry. Upside down, he burst out laughing, and then the "Hahaha!" wouldn't stop; laughing hurt the rib, and he laughed again, and it hurt again, laughing till he swung back and forth on the branch, for all the world a salted fish swinging in the wind.

Qi Changsong stood at the edge, drenched in sweat, Xiaoman's blood on his sleeve. He looked up at the child hanging upside down in the tree, a long time. "Twenty years," he said. "The first time my feet have left the ground." Then: "That charm of yours — where did it come from?" Xiaoman swung a little in the tree and answered upside down: "…Found it." Qi Changsong looked at him, said neither that he believed it nor that he didn't, gave him one nod, and walked down off the stage, and on the way he put out a hand and steadied the senior with the crooked topknot.
